idiom_name: Pundit authorize (raises unless the policy grants) with after_action :verify_authorized; Rails strong parameters
implementation_notes: Pundit makes denial the default at the call site: `authorize @post` instantiates the matching policy, calls the method for the current action and raises `Pundit::NotAuthorizedError` unless it returns true (the README's own expansion is `unless PostPolicy.new(current_user, @post).update? ... raise`). An action that forgets `authorize` is caught by `after_action :verify_authorized`, which the README describes as raising 'if authorize has not yet been called', with `verify_policy_scoped` covering index actions that use `policy_scope`. Rails contributes the same shape to input: `ActionController::Parameters#permit` keeps only the listed keys, and `permit_all_parameters` defaults to false, so mass assignment is allow-list by default. The grant set lives in policy classes (ApplicationPolicy subclasses) and controller filters such as `authenticate_user!` - ordinary, testable Ruby.
code_sketch:
class OrdersController < ApplicationController
  after_action :verify_authorized             # an action without authorize fails loudly
  def show
    @order = authorize Order.find(params[:id]) # raises unless the policy grants
    render json: @order
  end
  def order_params = params.expect(order: [:sku, :quantity])  # allow-list only
end
pitfalls: An action that never calls `authorize` (or never uses `policy_scope`) runs unguarded: enable `after_action :verify_authorized` and `verify_policy_scoped`, and treat `skip_authorization`/`skip_policy_scope` as exceptions that need a reason.

A `rescue_from Pundit::NotAuthorizedError` that logs and continues (or renders the page) converts denial into access; the rescue must end the request. Calling `authorize` with a class instead of the instance can also check the wrong policy.

`permit!`, `to_unsafe_h` and `ActionController::Parameters.permit_all_parameters = true` bypass the allow-list; the parameters API warns the class-level options are not thread-safe and should only be set once at boot, so a runtime toggle in a multi-threaded server is both a leak and a race.

Policy scopes are the list-path default: without `policy_scope(Order)` an index action returns the whole relation, and a scope that returns `scope.all` for convenience is the same fail-open in one line.

A policy that returns true for a missing record (NilClassPolicy-style tolerance) makes absence an allow path; keep such tolerance explicit and narrow, and note that an ApplicationPolicy initializer raising unless a user is present (the README's secondary defence) is the fail-closed alternative.
